lesson.title: The Building Blocks of an Experiment: Defining Experimental Units
lesson.summary: An experimental unit is the individual object, person, animal, or plot to which a single treatment is applied, and choosing this unit correctly at the level treatment is actually assigned is essential to an honest analysis.
lesson.body:
An experimental unit is the individual object, person, animal, plot, or item to which a single treatment is applied and on which a single measurement of the response is taken. Every experiment needs a clearly defined experimental unit before anything else can be decided, because the unit determines what counts as one independent piece of evidence.

In the fertilizer experiment described earlier, the experimental units were the 40 plots of land, since each plot individually received one version of fertilizer and produced one yield measurement. In a study of a new tire's wear resistance, the experimental units might be individual tires, or individual cars if tires are swapped as a full set. In a classroom study of a teaching method, the experimental units might be individual students, or entire classrooms if the teaching method is applied at the class level rather than to each student separately. The choice of unit is not automatic, it depends on the level at which the treatment is actually assigned.

Experimental units show up under different names depending on the field, which can make the underlying idea harder to spot at first. Agricultural scientists call them plots, manufacturing engineers might call them batches or production runs, chemists might call them samples, and clinical researchers eventually call human units subjects, a term the next section examines closely. Whatever the label, the underlying idea stays the same: an experimental unit is the smallest entity that could, in principle, have received a different treatment than the entity right next to it.

Getting the experimental unit right matters because the sample size used for statistical analysis should match the number of independently treated units, not the number of measurements taken. If a teaching method experiment assigns the new method to 3 classrooms and the standard method to 3 other classrooms, the experimental unit is the classroom, not the individual student, even if there are 25 students per classroom and 150 students total. Treating each of the 150 students as an independent experimental unit when the treatment was actually assigned at the classroom level inflates the apparent sample size and can make results look far more statistically convincing than the data actually support, since students in the same classroom share a teacher, environment, and peer effects and are not independent of one another.

Suppose the 3 classrooms using the new method average a 6 point score gain and the 3 classrooms using the standard method average a 2 point gain. The honest comparison is between 3 classroom averages and 3 other classroom averages, an effective sample size of 6 units, not 150. Reporting it as though it were based on 150 independent observations would badly overstate the precision of the estimate.

When the experimental units happen to be people, statisticians use a more specific term, subjects, precisely because human units bring additional concerns, such as consent and psychological response to treatment, that plots of land or tires do not. That distinction is the focus of the next section.
